positive_genai_teaching_experience: I have several assignments where students are working with messy data sources and trying to work toward well-formatted figures presenting that data. I have had students get stuck when the code they write produces an error message that they can't figure out. ChatGPT has been effective at helping them debug the code. In the past, a student would have typically waited until office hours and then I could spot the mistake in a few seconds and the student could then get back to work. ChatGPT performs a similar function but does so in real time for the student, letting them keep their momentum on the assignment rather than waiting for office hours or an email response from me.
negative_genai_teaching_experience: I had a student submit a referee report (a critical assessment of an academic article summarizing, critiquing and offering suggestions for improvement) that was clearly generated by AI. The referee report was written entirely in generalities and never engaged with any relevant details of the paper itself. Grading the report by my rubric led to a failing grade. Hopefully students start to realize that misusing GenAI won't necessarily be to their benefit.
major_genai_teaching_concerns: My biggest concern so far is that it requires a rethinking of open-book exams. In the past, when giving an open-book exam in class or as a take-home exam, I always allowed students to access their laptops to reference their notes, readings, lecture slides and so on. Now, after some clear cheating with GenAI (that led to really, really bad answers), I only allow them to access hardcopies which is frustratingly inefficient (lots of unnecessary printing and clutter during the exams).

positive_genai_teaching_experience: GenAI helped me revitalize my syllabus by helping me find new material to include. I used ChatGPT for brainstorming content to include in my syllabus. I think it was perhaps slightly more efficient than just using Google. But maybe it was more helpful than I realized at the time. I'm not sure how long it necessarily might have taken me using traditional tools like Google search.
negative_genai_teaching_experience: A negative example is the time that it now takes to craft an up-to-date policy regarding GenAI on my syllabus from semester to semester, and then the anxiety about policing use of AI on papers. I haven't suspected text generation yet in my student papers, but I now have to budget extra time for policing that when I plan for the time needed to grade papers.
major_genai_teaching_concerns:
Biggest concern I think is that, if it's as big a technological leap and sea change as all the exuberance and interest would indicate, my concern is that we may not adapt fast enough to help students keep apace with changes in career shifts, changes in the workplaces they will be entering after W&M, or that our core commitment to liberal arts values and skills (reading and writing for example) may be eroded (i.e. students and others coming to think that we don't need to learn to read or write anymore because these tools can do it for us). 
A second big concern is as I mentioned before the need to police the use of AI in student papers. It's an additional anxiety and time burden. Any tools that could streamline things for us could be really helpful.
A lesser anxiety is that we might, at least at present, commit too much time to adapting to this technological shift. I taught a course last semester about the history of technology in the nineteenth century and found myself constantly coming back to the implications and future of Gen AI, in part because talk of AI was everywhere, but also because I thought it was important for students to be critical and conscious of its implications from a historical, cultural, social, aesthetic and political standpoint in addition to the purely technical capabilities of the technology.

negative_genai_teaching_experience:
I suspect some students have used it -- against my course rules -- to generate discussion posts or ideas for their papers, as I've come across some completely fabricated quotations from primary sources, and a fair bit of incredibly generic and thoughtless ideas or writing, which goes completely against the purpose of the assignment.  

This is especially a problem in my courses that focus on well-known primary texts, where a key skill students are learning is doing their *own* analysis of those texts, and where I already did not permit any use of external sources. Because these are well-known primary texts, there's a lot of information about them in whatever data sources ChatGPT uses, so it can always spit something out, even if the quality is poor and generic and does not capture the nuances discussed this particular class. The very use of it, though, shortcuts the exact skills of thinking and analysis I'm trying to get students to learn and practice. 

I expect I'll be using a lot more in-class essay exams in the future to replace some at-home assignments, which is a shame because that in-class essay exams can be stressful for students. I am also finding that many assignments are going to require significant redesign to avoid students using ChatGPT to cheat on them.

major_genai_teaching_concerns: The students who are struggling and have limited time are the ones more likely to use it inappropriately and also more likely to suffer negative consequences. I had difficulty answering some of the survey questions because I have a policy for which assignments GenAI can be used for and which students may not use these tools.  So while, for example, where the use of ChatGPT can elminate the need for students to think deeply and creatively about how to even begin an assignment (a critical skill), I have specified that students cannot use GenAI for such assignments.  So, where GenAI can have a strong and adverse effect on learning, I have tried to control for that.  So, I didn't know whether to respond about the impact of GenAI in the context of my policies or as if there were no guardrails on GenAI.  That said, I am quite confident that I cannot expect every student to adhere to my policies and, regrettably, I have no control over that as I cannot be with every student 24 hours a day.  However, we try to make it abundantly clear that the use of GenAI can diminish or eliminate learning and those who are intent on learning, I think, adhere to my course policies.

Relying on code from ChatGPT will be determinantal to graduates' success because (1) they won't even know if the ChatGPT code is correct, (2) ChatGPT code is often incorrect, slow, or overly complex, (3) their skills will never be better than ChatGPT and so they will have no way to set themselves apart from those with whom they are competing.

positive_genai_teaching_experience: GenAI allowed students on a recent assignment to correctly apply a concept that was previously frequently missed. This is transformative, because, while correct application is important, what is arguably more important is a deep understanding of the underlying construct. GenAI allows us as educators to focus on higher-ordered learning, e.g., synthesis and integration...and innovation.
negative_genai_teaching_experience: I have also had students simply input the prompt of the assignment and copy and paste the output. We have had to become much more savvy as educators, while our assessments haven't changed...yet...our expectations of the submissions have. Written submissions without citations and the direct integration and application of specific concepts discussed in the course are now not acceptable. I try to set clear expectations. I assume all students are using GenAI and they are encouraged to do so but must fact-check the output and support all course-specific concepts with citations to course materials.
major_genai_teaching_concerns: Resistance to adoption by faculty and an unchecked covert use by students. Both players should adopt GenAI and consider how to leverage it as a tool...responsibly.

major_genai_teaching_concerns: We just don't yet know how Gen AI will impact students' cognitive and creative skills. So, while we may hope that it will benefit them we just don't know without conducting research studies. So, this is all a big experiment at this point. Therefore, I think we should proceed with cautious optimism, healthy skepticism, and a clear-eyed view.
